title: Master R & ggplot2 Data Visualization
text:
Quick-start
Install everything at once:
pkgs <- c(
  "ggplot2", "ggthemes", "hrbrthemes", "ggdark",
  "patchwork", "ggrepel", "ggtext", "gridExtra",
  "cowplot", "scales", "tidyverse"
)
install.packages(pkgs)
Your first ggplot2 plot:
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, lwd = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#e84855", "#2d6be4", "#12a36a")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Vehicle Weight vs Fuel Economy",
    subtitle = "Grouped by number of cylinders · mtcars dataset",
    x        = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
    y        = "Miles per Gallon",
    colour   = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: ggplot2
text:
ggplot2 is a powerful and widely-used open-source of data visualization library for the R programming language. It is based on the grammar of graphics, a concept developed by Hardly Wickham in his book “The Grammar of Graphics”. It is a general framework for creating statistical graphics. The grammar of graphics provides a flexible and systematic approach to creating complex plots, making it easy to create and customize a wide variety of visualizations.
One of the key features of ggplot2 is its ability to create layered plots. Each layer in a ggplot2 plot represents a different aspect of the data, such as points, lines, or bars. Layers can be added or removed from a plot to change its appearance and convey different information.
For example, consider a simple scatter plot of height and weight data for a group of individuals. To create this plot using ggplot2, you would first use the “ggplot()” function to create a new plot object, and then use the “aes()” function to define the x and y variables. Next, you would use the “geom_point()” function to add a layer of points to the plot.
We can install ggplot2 just by using the command
install.packages("ggplot2")
The basic syntax for creating a plot with ggplot2 is:
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_*()
Where:
ggplot(): The main function used to create a new plot object. It takes a data frame as the first argument and an aesthetic mapping as the second argument.
data: It is a data frame containing the data to be plotted, “x” and “y” are the variables to be plotted on the x and y axes, respectively
aes(): Defines the mapping between variables in the data and visual elements of the plot. It takes one or more variables as arguments, and maps them to the x and y axes, as well as other aesthetics such as color, size, and shape.
geom_(): geom_ or geom function is the geometric object used to create the plot. geom funtion is a family of functions used to add different types of layers to a plot. These include geom_point() for scatter plots, geom_line() for line plots, geom_bar() for bar charts, and many others.
There are many different types of geometric objects that can be used in ggplot2, including:
geom_point(): creates a scatter plot geom_line(): creates a line plot geom_bar(): creates a bar chart geom_histogram(): creates a histogram geom_boxplot(): creates a boxplot geom_density(): creates a density plot geom_blank() creates a blank plot
geom_boxplot(): creates a Box plot
geom_density() creates a Density plot
geom_dotplot() creates a Dot plot
geom_map() creates a Map plot
geom_polygon() creates a Polygons plot
geom_ribbon() or geom_area() creates a Ribbons and area plot
geom_segment() or geom_curve() creates a Line segments and curves plot
geom_smooth() or stat_smooth() creates a Conditional means plot
geom_label() or geom_text() creates a Text plot
geom_violin() creates a Violin plot
Each geometric object can be customized with additional arguments, such as the color and size of the points or lines, the fill color of the bars, etc.
For example, the following code creates a scatter plot of the “mtcars” data set, with the “mpg” (Miles per Gallon) variable on the x-axis and the “wt” (weight) variable on the y-axis:

library(ggplot2)

data(mtcars)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point()

The above code will create a scatter plot of vs .
Additionally, you can customize the appearance of the plot by adding various other layers and elements. For example, you can add a linear regression line to the plot using the “geom_smooth()” function, and change the color and size of the points using the “size” and “color” aesthetics.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

In this example, the linear regression line is added to the plot using the “geom_smooth()” function, and the points are made smaller and colored blue.
ggplot2 also allows for faceting, which can be used to create multiple plots based on one or more variables in the data.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ gear)

Another important aspect of ggplot2 is the ability to easily add various types of scales to a plot. Scales control the mapping between the data and the visual elements of the plot, such as the axis labels and tick marks. ggplot2 provides a variety of scales, including linear, logarithmic, and date scales.
For example, to create a bar chart of the number of cylinders for each model of car in the mtcars dataset, we can use the “geom_bar()” function and the “scale_x_discrete()” function to change the x-axis scale from continuous to discrete.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Number of Cylinders")

This code will create a bar chart with the x-axis labeled “Number of Cylinders” and the y-axis labeled “Count”. The bars will be separated by the number of cylinders and the count of the cars with that number of cylinder.
ggplot2 also provides a wide range of options for customizing the appearance of the plot, such as the axis labels, title, legend, etc.
ggplot2 also provides a variety of options for customizing the appearance of the plot, such as the “theme()” function, which can be used to change the font, color, and other elements of the plot.
ggplot2 has a wide variety of functions that can be used to create different types of plots and customize their appearance. Some of the main functions include:
scale_(): A family of functions used to add and customize scales to a plot. These include scale_x_() and scale_y_() functions for the x and y axes, respectively, as well as scale_color_(), scale_size_*(), and others for other aesthetics.
facet_*(): A family of functions used to create faceted plots. These include facet_wrap() and facet_grid(), which divide the plot into multiple smaller plots based on one or more variables.
theme(): Allows for customization of the overall appearance of the plot, including the background color and gridlines, font size, axis labels, and more.
labs(): Allows for customization of the plot labels, including the title, axis labels, and legend.
coord_*(): A family of functions used to change the coordinate system of the plot. For example, coord_flip() will flip the x and y axes, coord_polar() will change the plot to a polar coordinate system.
annotate(): Allows you to add text, shapes, and lines to the plot to highlight specific observations or provide additional information.
ggtitle() : Allows you to add a title to the plot.
xlab() and ylab() : Allows you to add labels to the x and y axis of the plot.
scale_*_*() : A family of functions used to customize the scales of the plot, like scale_color_gradient() and scale_x_log10()
stat_*() : A family of functions used to add summary statistics to the plot, like stat_smooth() and stat_summary()
These are some of the most commonly used functions in ggplot2, but there are many more that can be used to create and customize a wide variety of plots. The best way to learn how to use ggplot2 is to experiment with the different functions and see how they work.
The theme function allows you to customize many aspects of the overall appearance of the plot such as background color, gridlines, font size, axis labels, and more. For example, to remove the background gridlines and change the axis labels to a smaller font size, you can use the following code:
scss Copy code ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme( panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
The theme() function in ggplot2 allows you to customize many aspects of the overall appearance of the plot, such as the background color, gridlines, font size, axis labels, and more. It takes a series of element_*() functions as arguments, each of which corresponds to a different aspect of the plot.
For example, to remove the background gridlines and change the axis labels to a smaller font size, you can use the following code:
scss Copy code ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme( panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8) ) The element_blank() function is used to remove the gridlines, and the element_text() function is used to change the font size of the axis labels.
Other common element_*() functions include:
element_line(): Allows you to customize the appearance of lines, such as the axis lines and gridlines.
element_rect(): Allows you to customize the appearance of rectangles, such as the background of the plot.
element_text(): Allows you to customize the appearance of text, such as the axis labels and legend titles.
element_blank(): Allows you to remove elements from the plot.
You can also use theme_set() to set a pre-defined theme. The most common ones are theme_gray(), theme_bw(), theme_light(), theme_dark() and

Theme
The ggplot2 package have different themes. By default it uses the theme_grey (theme_gray()), so we don’t need to specify it. Themes provided by ggplot are below
theme_gray() – default ggplot2 theme with a grey background and white gridlines
theme_bw() – dark and light (black and white) ggplot2 theme
theme_linedraw() – uses black lines on white backgrounds only
theme_light() – similar to linedraw() but with grey lines
theme_dark() – lines on a dark background
theme_minimal() – no background annotations
theme_classic() – theme with no grid lines
theme_void() – empty theme with no elements
We can also modify the plot base size by using base_size argument in the theme functions.

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

# Scatter Plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() ->p

p+ facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw(base_size=20)->p1
p1

## theme_dark()
p+theme_dark()->p2
p2



Lab funtion
Whit using of labs() function we can set a title, subtitle, caption, and axis title of the plot.

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

# Scatter Plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() ->p

p+ facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw(base_size=20)->p

## Lab Function
p+labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot",
       caption = "Caption of the plot",
       x = "x-axis",
       y = "y-axis")->p
p



Modify plot with theme function
We can modify our plot with the use of `theme() function. Here we can define position of the title, subtile, caption, panel background, legend position, and many more things. You can define your own theme, size, color, shape of the plot as you want. Below given some use theme arguments which are also my favorite
theme(
  axis.title,        ## for both axis
  axis.title.x,      ## for x axis
  axis.title.y,      ## for y axis
  axis.text,         ## for both axis
  axis.text.x,       ## for x axis
  axis.text.y,       ## for y axis
  axis.ticks,        ## for both axis
  axis.ticks.x,      ## for x axis
  axis.ticks.y,      ## for y axis
  axis.line,         ## for both axis
  axis.line.x,       ## for x axis
  axis.line.y,       ## for y axis
  legend.background,
  legend.margin,
  legend.text,
  legend.title,
  legend.position,
  legend.direction,
  legend.box,
  panel.background,
  panel.border,
  panel.grid,
  panel.grid.major,
  panel.grid.minor,
  plot.background,
  plot.title,
  plot.subtitle,
  plot.caption,
  plot.tag,
  plot.margin,
  strip.background,
  strip.background.x,
  strip.background.y,
  strip.text,
  strip.text.x,
  strip.text.y)
With the using of these arguments we are able to modify plot, these arguments
element_line() use for line
element_rect() use for color
element_text() use for text
element_blank() use for blank
For example
theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 1),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 0.5),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "yellow"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 2))

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

# Scatter Plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  geom_point() ->p

p+ facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme of the plot
p+theme_bw()->p

## Lab Function
p+labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot",
       caption = "Caption of the plot")->p

## theme function
p+theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(family = "serif",              # Font family
                                  face = "bold",                 # Font face
                                  size = 15,                     # Font size
                                  hjust = 1,                     # Horizontal adjustment
                                  vjust = 1),                   # Vertical adjustment
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 1),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.1),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "yellow"),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 2),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "pink"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "green"),
        panel.border = element_rect(linetype = "dashed"),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "black"))->p 
p



Combine multiple plot
The ggplot2 package doesn’t providing function to arrange multiples plots in a single figure, but there are some packages, that allow combine multiples plots into a single figure with custom layouts, width, height, such as cowplot, gridExtra, patchwork. (https://medium.com/@pawanjangra1198/combining-plots-in-ggplot2-9699acaa2942#6632-36f5b0859cff)

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

# Scatter Plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() ->p

p+ facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw(base_size=20)->p1
p1

## theme_dark()
p+theme_dark()->p2
p2

The gridExtra package provides the grid.arrange function to combine several plots on a single figure.

# install.packages("gridExtra")
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

# Combine the plots with gridExtra
grid.arrange(p1, p2) 



Save plot
We can save the plot by using ggsave() function and in this we can define the height, width of the plot.

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

# Scatter Plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() ->p

p+ facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw(base_size=20)->p

## save the plot
ggsave("~/ggplot/plot.png", width = 3200, height = 2800, unit = "px")

title: Geom Functions
text: Geoms are the geometric objects used to represent data. Every geom function starts with geom_. You can stack multiple geoms in one plot by chaining them with +.

title: Geom Functions
text:
Scatter — geom_point()
library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Colour, size, alpha
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8)

# Add regression line
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "tomato")

# Bubble chart — size mapped to data
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 12))

title: Geom Functions
text:
Lines — geom_line() / geom_path()
# Time-series line chart
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()

# Styled line
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2d6be4", linewidth = 1)

# Multiple lines by group
ggplot(economics_long, aes(x = date, y = value01, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line()

# Step line (useful for step-wise data)
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_step()

# geom_path — connects in data order (not sorted by x)
ggplot(economics, aes(x = unemploy/pop, y = psavert)) +
  geom_path(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Unemployment rate", y = "Personal savings rate")

title: Geom Functions
text:
Bars — geom_bar() / geom_col()
# Count bars (default stat="count")
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar()

# Identity bars (pre-summarised)
df <- data.frame(group = LETTERS[1:4], values = c(5,2,7,2))

ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = values)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

# geom_col — shorthand for stat="identity"
ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = values, fill = group)) +
  geom_col()

# Horizontal with coord_flip
ggplot(df, aes(x = values, y = reorder(group, values))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2d6be4")

# With value labels on top
ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = values)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = values), vjust = -0.4, fontface = "bold")

title: Geom Functions
text:
Histogram — geom_histogram()
# Basic histogram
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10)

# Custom bin width & fill
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white")

# Density overlay
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#c3e7ff", colour = "white", bins = 12) +
  geom_density(colour = "#2d6be4", linewidth = 1)

# Multiple groups
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, binwidth = 2, position = "identity")

title: Geom Functions
text:
Density — geom_density()
# Basic density
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)

# Multiple groups
cyls <- as.factor(mtcars$cyl)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

# 2D density heat map
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = "white", size = 1.5)

title: Geom Functions
text:
Boxplot — geom_boxplot()
# Basic boxplot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot()

# Coloured fill + notches
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, outlier.colour = "tomato", outlier.size = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# With jittered points overlaid
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = factor(cyl)), width = 0.15, size = 2, alpha = 0.7)

title: Geom Functions
text:
Violin — geom_violin()
# Basic violin
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6)

# Violin + boxplot combo
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "MPG")

# Half violin — gghalves package
# install.packages("gghalves")
# library(gghalves)
# ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
#   geom_half_violin() + geom_half_point()

title: Geom Functions
text:
Area — geom_area() / geom_ribbon()
# Area chart
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5), colour = "#2d6be4")

# Ribbon — shaded confidence band
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = unemploy - 500, ymax = unemploy + 500),
              fill = "#2d6be4", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = unemploy), colour = "#2d6be4")

# Stacked area chart
library(tidyr)
economics_long |>
  dplyr::filter(variable %in% c("pce","pop")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value01, fill = variable)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7, position = "stack")

title: Geom Functions
text:
Heatmap — geom_tile() / geom_raster()
# Correlation matrix heatmap
library(tidyr)

cor_df <- as.data.frame(cor(mtcars))
cor_df$var1 <- rownames(cor_df)
cor_long <- pivot_longer(cor_df, -var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "corr")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = corr)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2d6be4", mid = "white", high = "#e84855", midpoint = 0
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "mtcars Correlation Matrix", fill = "r")

# Calendar heatmap style
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = color, fill = carat)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c()

title: Geom Functions
text:
Smooth trend — geom_smooth()
# Default LOESS smooth
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

# Linear regression
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "tomato")

# By group
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

# method options: "lm", "glm", "gam", "loess", "rlm"

title: Geom Functions
text:
Jitter — geom_jitter()
# Avoid overplotting in categorical data
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, colour = "steelblue", size = 2, alpha = 0.7)

# geom_jitter is shorthand for geom_point(position = position_jitter())
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +

text:
Data Frames
A data frame is R’s tabular data structure — like a spreadsheet. Each column is a vector; all columns have equal length.
Syntax: df[row, column] — first argument = row, second = column.
# Create a data frame
data.frame(
  x = 1:7,
  y = c("Sun","Mon","Tue","Wed","Thurs","Fri","Sat")
) -> df
df

# Access columns
df[ , 2]      # all rows, column 2
df$x          # column x by name (returns vector)
df[2,  ]      # all columns of row 2
df[1:3, 1]    # rows 1–3, column 1

# Useful info
nrow(df)      # number of rows
ncol(df)      # number of columns
dim(df)       # c(rows, cols)
str(df)       # structure overview
head(df)      # first 6 rows
tail(df)      # last 6 rows
summary(df)   # descriptive statistics
names(df)     # column names
colnames(df)  # same as names

df1 <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = c("a","b","c"), z = 12:14)
df2 <- data.frame(x = 4:6, y = c("A","B","C"), z = 21:23)

rbind(df1, df2)   # by rows   (stacked)       — same column names required

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text: When using ggplot2 you can set a title, a subtitle, a caption in the plot. There are two ways to add title, subtitle (i) using ggtitle, (ii) using labs function.

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Title
Let’s adding a title of the plot in ggplot2 with ggtitle

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  ggtitle("Title of the plot using ggtitle()") 


Option 2. Using labs
You can also use the labs function to add the title.

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title of the plot using labs()") 



Title position
The title position can be set respect to the whole plot instead of the panel with the plot.title.position component of the theme function. Default value is “panel”. This configuration also applies to the subtitle.

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title on the plot margin") + 
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Subtitle
You can add a subtitle the same way you added the title, but with the subtitle argument.

Option 1. Using ggtitle
Add a subtitle in ggplot2

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) +  
  ggtitle("Title of the plot",
          subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot") 



Option 2. Using labs
Subtitle in ggplot2 using labs

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot")

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Caption
A caption can be used to describe the figure. You can add it with the caption argument of the labs function.
Adding a caption in ggplot2

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot",
       caption = "This is the caption") 

The plot.caption.position of the theme function allows aliging the caption to the panel (“panel”, default) or the whole plot (“plot”).

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(caption = "This is the caption") +
  theme(plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 

Changing the caption position in ggplot2
Note that the default for the caption is right alignment, so you can set hjust = 0 to move the caption to the left of the whole plot.

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Tag
Adding a tag to the plot in ggplot2
Tags are useful to indicate the figure numbering. You can add it with the tag argument of the labs function.

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot",
       caption = "This is the caption",
       tag = "Fig. 1") 


Tag position
Changing the tag position in ggplot2
The position of the tag can be set with the plot.tag.position component of the theme function. Possible values are “topleft” (default), “top”, “topright”, “left”, “right”, “bottomleft”, “bottom” or “bottomright”.

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(tag = "Fig. 1") +
  theme(plot.tag.position = "bottomright")

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Further styles and adjustments
The titles, subtitles, captions and tags can be customized with the plot.title, plot.subtitle, plot.caption and plot.tag components of the theme function, making use of element_text. You can modify the color, the font family, the text size, the text face, the angle or the vertical and horizontal adjustment for each text as in the example below.
Styling the titles in ggplot2, such as modifying the color, size, face, family, lineheight and margins

# install.packages(ggplot2)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = rgb(0, 0.5, 1, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  labs(title = "Title of the plot",
       subtitle = "Subtitle of the plot",
       caption = "This is the caption",
       tag = "Fig. 1") + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(family = "serif",              # Font family
                                  face = "bold",                 # Font face
                                  color = 4,                     # Font color
                                  size = 15,                     # Font size
                                  hjust = 1,                     # Horizontal adjustment
                                  vjust = 1,                     # Vertical adjustment
                                  angle = -10,                   # Font angle
                                  lineheight = 1,                # Line spacing
                                  margin = margin(20, 0, 0, 0)), # Margins (t, r, b, l)
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0),                 # Subtitle customization
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.25),               # Caption customization
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "italic"),                # Tag customization
        plot.title.position = "plot",                            # Title and subtitle position ("plot" or "panel")
        plot.caption.position = "panel",                         # Caption position ("plot" or "panel")
        plot.tag.position = "top")                               # Tag position

title: ggplot2 : title, subtitle, and caption
text:
Plot border color
Changing the colors with themes Color picker Default plot
By default, ggplot2 plots have a gray panel and a white background.

library(ggplot2)

# Sample data
set.seed(123)
x <- 1:220
y <- x + rnorm(220, sd = 50)

df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Plot
ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point()

Default background color in ggplot2
Panel background color You can change the panel background color setting an element_rect in the panel.background component of the theme function as follows.
Change the background panel color in ggplot2

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = cyl))+ 
  geom_point() + 
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#67c9ff")) 

Panel border color Option 1
ggplot2 panel border color
The panel.border component of the theme function controls the color and width of the border of the panel with the color and size arguments. However, you will need to set fill = “transparent” to avoid hiding the data.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = "transparent", # Needed to add the border
                                    color = 4,            # Color of the border
                                    size = 2))            # Border width 

Option 2
Border color of the plot in ggplot2
You can also set a element_rect for the panel.background component and modify the border color with the color argument. However, this is not the recommended workflow, as it doesn’t override the current border. You can check this with theme_bw (Note that the black border is behind the blue border).

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(color = 4, # Color of the border
                                        size = 2)) # Border width 

Plot background color The plot.background component of the theme function allows modifying the background color of the figure. Set the color inside the fill argument of an element_rect.
Plot background color in ggplot2

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = cyl))+ 
  geom_point() + 
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "gray86")) # Background color of the plot 

Plot border color Plot border color in ggplot
You can also set a border color for the whole figure. Just pass an element_rect to the plot.background component of the theme function and modify the color and the width of the border with the arguments color and size, respectively.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(color = "black", # Border color
                                       size = 2))       # Border width 

Changing the colors with themes It is worth mentioning that there are lots of ggplot themes available that provide different background colors.
In this example we are setting the theme_dark, which is one of the in-built ggplot2 themes.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_dark() 

Note that the default theme is theme_grey.
Change the color of a plot with a ggplot theme
Color picker Use the color pickers to change the panel color (left) and the plot color (right), or to generate random colors pressing the blue button. Then you can copy the colors and use them in your plots.

title: How to Draw
text:
How to Draw a Barplot in R (5 Examples)
This tutorial illustrates how to create a barchart in R programming.
I will explain how to plot barplots using Base R as well as using the ggplot2 add-on package. Furthermore, I’ll demonstrate how to draw stacked and grouped barcharts.
Let’s start right away!
Construction of Example Data Before all else, let’s create some example data in R.

df1 <- data.frame(values = c(5, 2, 7, 2),              # Create example data frame
                  group = LETTERS[1:4])
df1

As you can see based on the previous RStudio console output, our example data is a data frame containing four rows and two columns. The variable values has the numeric class and the variable group is a character.
Example 1: Create Barchart Using Base R In this example, I’ll show how to draw barcharts using the basic installation of the R programming language.
If we want to create a Base R barplot with default specifications, we can apply the code as shown below:

barplot(values ~ group,                                # Draw Base R barplot
        df1)

r graph figure 1 draw barplot
As shown in Figure 1, we have created a bargraph with vertical gray bars.
We can modify the alignment of the bars using the horiz argument:

barplot(values ~ group,                                # Horizontal barplot
        df1,
        horiz = TRUE)

r graph figure 2 draw barplot
By executing the previous R code, we have created Figure 2, i.e. a barplot with horizontal bars.
We can also change the colors of our barplot:

barplot(values ~ group,                                # Barplot with colors
        df1,
        col = 1:4)

r graph figure 3 draw barplot
The output of the previous R code is shown in Figure 3: A barplot with a different color in each bar.
If we want to add a legend on top of this barchart, we can apply the legend function as shown below:
legend("topright",                                     # Add legend to barplot
       df1$group,
       fill = 1:4)
r graph figure 4 draw barplot
As revealed in Figure 4, the previous R programming syntax has added a legend on top of our Base R barchart.
Base R provides many further options on how to manipulate our barcharts. However, I want to move on to a very common add-on package for graphics in R – the ggplot2 package!
Example 2: Create Barchart Using ggplot2 Package The following syntax explains how to use the ggplot2 package to draw basically the same types of barcharts as in the previous section.
First, we need to install and load the ggplot2 package:

## install.packages("ggplot2")                            # Install & load ggplot2
library("ggplot2")

Next, we can draw a ggplot2 barplot with default setting as shown below:

ggplot(df1,                                            # Draw ggplot2 barplot
       aes(x = group,
           y = values)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

r graph figure 5 draw barplot
As shown in Figure 5, we have created a vertical barchart without colors by executing the previous R syntax.
If we want to draw a horizontal bargraph, we can apply the coord_flip function as shown below:

ggplot(df1,                                            # Horizontal barplot
       aes(x = group,
           y = values)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip()

r graph figure 6 draw barplot
By executing the previously shown R code, we have created Figure 6, i.e. a horizontally aligned bargraph.
We can also add colors and a legend to our barplot by using the fill argument within the aesthetics of our ggplot2 plot:

ggplot(df1,                                            # Barplot with colors
       aes(x = group,
           y = values,
           fill = group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

r graph figure 7 draw barplot
In Figure 7 you can see that we have plotted a colored ggplot2 barplot using the previous R programming syntax.
So far, so good – Let’s draw some more advanced barplots!
Example 3: Create Stacked Barchart Using ggplot2 Package The following sections explain how to visualize more complex data, i.e. data with main and subgroups, in a barplot.
First, we have to create another data set:

df2 <- data.frame(values = c(3, 2, 6, 3, 4, 3, 8, 2),  # Data frame with subgroups
                  maingroup = rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 2),
                  subgroup = letters[1:2])
df2                                                    # Print new data frame

In the previous console output you can see that we have created another data set with the previous R code. This data set contains three columns, a values column as well as a main and sub group indicator.
We can now visualize these data in a so called stacked barplot, i.e. where the subgroups are plotted on top of each other within the same bar:

ggplot(df2,                                            # Draw stacked barplot
       aes(x = maingroup,
           y = values,
           fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

r graph figure 8 draw barplot
By running the previous syntax, we have created Figure 8, i.e. a stacked ggplot2 barchart.
Example 4: Create Stacked Barchart Scaled to 100% Using ggplot2 Package To make the comparison between the subgroups more visual, we may scale the bars in our barplot to the same height.
This code demonstrates how to scale all bars to the value 1:

ggplot(df2,                                            # Scale to 1.0
       aes(x = maingroup,
           y = values,
           fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity",
           position = "fill")

r graph figure 9 draw barplot
As shown in Figure 9, we have created a barplot scaled to 1.
Alternatively, we may scale all bars to 100%:

ggplot(df2,                                            # Scale to 100%
       aes(x = maingroup,
           y = values,
           fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity",
           position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format())

r graph figure 10 draw barplot
The output of the previous syntax is shown in Figure 10: The stacked bars are exactly the same as in the previous graph. However, the y-axis was changed to percentage points.
Example 5: Create Grouped Barchart Using ggplot2 Package Another very popular way to visualize subgroups are so called grouped barplots.
We can use the ggplot2 package to draw a grouped barplot as shown below. Note that the following R code specifies the position argument within the geom_bar function to be equal to “dodge”:

ggplot(df2,                                            # Draw grouped barplot
       aes(x = maingroup,
           y = values,
           fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity",
           position = "dodge")

r graph figure 11 draw barplot
As visualized in Figure 11, the previous R programming code has created a grouped ggplot2 barplot.

title: ggplot2-theme
text:
Themes in ggplot2
The ggplot2 package have different themes. By default it uses the theme_grey (theme_gray()), so we don’t need to specify it.
We can adjusted themes by adding an in-build theme from ggplot2.
theme_gray() – default ggplot2 theme with a grey background and white gridlines
theme_bw() – dark and light (black and white) ggplot2 theme
theme_linedraw() – uses black lines on white backgrounds only
theme_light() – similar to linedraw() but with grey lines
theme_dark() – lines on a dark background
theme_minimal() – no background annotations
theme_classic() – theme with no grid lines
theme_void() – empty theme with no elements
We can also modify the plot base size by using base_size argument in the theme functions.

library(ggplot2)

iris->dataset

## Bar plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, fill = Species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw(base_size=20) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p1
p1

## theme_dark()
p+theme_dark() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p2 

p2



ggthemes package
The ggthemes package contains several very popular themes.
theme_base()         theme_cala()                  theme_clean()
theme_economist()    theme_excel()                 theme_excel_new()
theme_few()          theme_fivethirtyeight()       theme_foundation()
theme_gdocs()        theme_hc()                    theme_igray()
theme_map()          theme_pander()                theme_par()
theme_solarized()    theme_solid()                 theme_stata()

library(ggplot2)
## install.packages("ggthemes")
library(ggthemes)

iris->dataset

## Bar plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, fill = Species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~Species)->p

## theme_base()
p+theme_base() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p1

## theme_economist()
p+theme_economist() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p2
p1
p2



hrbrthemes package
hrbrthemes provides typography-centric themes and theme components for ggplot2. The available themes are listed below,
theme_ipsum()              theme_ipsum_es()             theme_ipsum_rc()
theme_ipsum_ps()           theme_ipsum_pub()            theme_ipsum_tw()
theme_ipsum_modern_rc()    theme_ft_rc()

library(ggplot2)
## install.apckages("hrbrthemes")
library(hrbrthemes)

iris->dataset

## Bar plot
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, fill = Species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~Species)->p

p+theme_ipsum()  +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p
p



ggdark package
ggdark provides the dark mode themes of the ggplot2 themes. This package can convert any theme into a dark theme. The available themes are listed below.
dark_theme_gray()         dark_theme_linedraw()          dark_theme_light()          dark_theme_dark()         dark_theme_minimal()           dark_theme_classic()        dark_theme_void()         dark_mode()

library(ggplot2)
## install.packages("ggdark")
library(ggdark)

mtcars->dt
cyls <- as.factor(dt$cyl)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7)->p

p+dark_theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p1 
p1
p+dark_theme_linedraw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p2 
p2



mdthemes
mdthemes contains all the themes provided by ggplot2, ggthemes, hrbrthemes, and other themes packages. Like as below
md_theme_grey()

md_theme_bw()

md_theme_linedraw()

md_theme_light()

md_theme_dark()

md_theme_minimal()

md_theme_classic()

library(ggplot2)
# install.packages("mdthemes")
library(mdthemes)
mtcars->dt
cyls <- as.factor(dt$cyl)

ggplot(dt, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7)->p
p+labs(title = "**Plot title**",
       subtitle = "*Plot subtitle*")->p

## theme_bw()
p+theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p1
p1

## md_theme_linedraw()
p+md_theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")->p2 

p2



ggthemr package
Note that you will need to call ggthemr_reset() to reset to the default ggplot2 theme.
The ggthemr package works different than the other packages. Instead of using the theme function and set a theme you can set a theme globally making use of the ggthemr function and passing the theme as string as argument.
ggthemr("flat")           ggthemr("flat dark")          ggthemr("camouflage")
ggthemr("carrot")         ggthemr("chalk")              ggthemr("copper")
ggthemr("dust")           ggthemr("earth")              ggthemr("fresh")
ggthemr("grape")          ggthemr("grass")              ggthemr("greyscale")
ggthemr("light")          ggthemr("lilac")              ggthemr("pale")
ggthemr("sea")            ggthemr("sky")                ggthemr("solarized")

library(ggplot2)
##devtools::install_github('Mikata-Project/ggthemr')
library(ggthemr)

mtcars->dt
cyls <- as.factor(dt$cyl)

ggthemr("flat")

ggplot(dt, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")



ggtech package
The ggtech package provides themes inspired by tech companies, such as Airbnb, Google, Twitter or Facebook.
theme_tech(theme="airbnb")               theme_tech(theme="etsy")
theme_tech(theme="facebook")             theme_tech(theme="google")
theme_tech(theme="tiwtter")              theme_airbnb_fancy()

library(ggplot2)
##devtools::install_github("ricardo-bion/ggtech",
##                          dependencies=TRUE)
library(ggtech)

mtcars->dt
cyls <- as.factor(dt$cyl)

ggplot(dt, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
  ggtitle("Title of the plot") +
  theme_tech(theme = "airbnb") +
  scale_fill_tech(theme = "airbnb") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

ggplot(dt, aes(x = mpg, fill = cyls)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
  ggtitle("Title of the plot") +
  theme_tech(theme = "facebook") +
  scale_fill_tech(theme = "facebook") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text: The ggplot2 package doesn’t providing function to arrange multiples plots in a single figure, but there are some packages, that allow combine multiples plots into a single figure with custom layouts, width, height, such as cowplot, gridExtra, patchwork

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Combining ggplot2 plots
patchwork is designed to combine ggplot2 plots into the same figure easily with using the + operator to combine the charts.

# install.packages("patchwork")
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots
p1 + p2

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Controlling the layout
If you want to customize the number of rows or columns of the figure you can use the plot_layout function. Also you can also specify the widths and heights of the plots with widths and heights arguments.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3) 

The most interesting functionality of the plot_layout function is that you can create a custom layout design as shown in the example below, where 1, 2, 3 and 4 represents the locations for p1,p2, p3 and p4, respectively, and # represents an empty space. Recall that you can use numbers but also letters to represent the plot locations.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots with a custom layout
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_layout(design ="111
                       2#3
                       443") 


The wrap_plots function
Sometimes you can’t use the + operator programatically, so if you don’t know the number of plots beforehand you can use the wrap_plots function and pass a list of plots to it. This function also allows specifying the number of rows and columns, the sizes and the custom layouts.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots
wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4, 
           ncol = 2, nrow = 2,
           widths = c(1, 0.5), heights = c(0.5, 1)) 



Adding spacers
When creating a custom layout you can use # to add spaces, as shown in one of the previous examples, but if you are using + there is also a function named plot_spacer to add spaces or gaps between plots.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Plots with spaces
p1 + plot_spacer() + plot_spacer() + p3

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Operators
The patchwork package also provides two operators to place plots beside each other or to stack them.

Arranging ggplot2 plots in rows (beside each other)
The | operator places plots in a row. This operator is similar to + when you have two plots but | will place all plots in a single row while + will try to create a square layout if possible.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots in rows
p1 | p2



Arranging ggplot2 plots in columns (stacked)
The / operator stacks the ggplot2 plots into columns without the need of using the plot_layout function and specifying ncol = 1.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Combine the plots as column
p1 / p2

You can create complex layouts. The | and / operators can be use to create complex layouts combining plots. In the following example we are creating a layout with two plots at the top and one wider at the bottom.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Two plots on top and one at the bottom
(p1 | p2) / p3 

The following example is similar to the previous, but with one plot at the left and two at the right.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# One plot at the left and two at the right
p1 | (p2 / p3)

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Titles and labels

Title for all the plots
You can add a title, subtitle and captions to all plots with the plot_annotation function.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Title for the combined plots
p1 + ((p2 | p3) / p4) + 
plot_annotation(title = "Title",
                subtitle = "Subtitle",
                caption = "Caption") 

The plot_annotation function can also be used to label each plot individually with the tags_level argument. Possible options are “1” for numbers, “a” for lowercase letters, “A” for uppercase letters, “i” for lowercase Roman numerals, “I” for uppercase Roman numerals or a vector with your own tags.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Labels for each plot
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") 

The labels can be customized with the tag_prefix, tag_suffix and tag_sep arguments.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Labels for each plot
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A", tag_prefix = "Plot ")

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Adding more layers
The figures created with patchwork behave the same way as a ggplot2 object, so you can add new layers as with normal plots, but the layer will be applied to the last added plot.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Add a new layer
p2 + p1 +
  geom_jitter(color = "blue")

# Equivalent to:
p <- p2 + p1
p + geom_jitter(color = "blue") 

If you want to customize other than the last plot added you can add the new layer to it or save the patchwork, access the desired element and customize it, as shown in the following example.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Add a new layer to the first plot
p2 + theme_bw() + p1

# Equivalent to:
p <- p2 + p1
p[[1]] <- p[[1]] + theme_bw()
p


Modifying all plots at the same time
patchwork also provides the & operator to modify all the plots at the same time to set the same theme for all plots at the same time.

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Change the theme for all plots
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 & theme_classic()

title: Combining plots in ggplot2
text:
Adding tables and text
When adding base R plots and ggplot2 plots patchwork won’t be able to align the plots, so you will need to customize the margins for one of the plots and try to fine tune the values until you reach a good alignment.
Making use of the tableGrob function from the gridExtra package you can add a table to a layout created with patchwork.

# install.packages("gridExtra")
library(ggplot2)

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_cartesian() — zoom without clipping
coord_cartesian() zooms into a region without removing data outside the view (unlike xlim() / ylim() which remove data and affect statistical calculations).
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

# Full plot
p

# Zoom in on x: 2–4, y: 15–30  (data outside still used for smooth)
p + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2, 4), ylim = c(15, 30))

# Compare — xlim() REMOVES data; affects the smooth line
p + xlim(2, 4) + ylim(15, 30)






Importantcoord_cartesian() vs xlim() / ylim()



coord_cartesian() zooms — all data is still used for statistical layers like geom_smooth().
xlim() / ylim() filter — data outside the range is dropped, which can distort stat layers.


# Expand ratio (add padding around data)
p + coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE)          # remove padding
p + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1.5, 5.5),
                    ylim = c(10, 35),
                    expand = FALSE)          # tight zoom, no padding

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_flip() — swap axes
Useful for horizontal bar charts, boxplots, and any chart where switching x/y improves readability.
library(ggplot2)

# Vertical bar chart (default)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar()

# Horizontal bar chart with coord_flip
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip()

# Horizontal sorted bar chart
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = reorder(rownames(mtcars), mpg), y = mpg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Miles per Gallon",
       title = "Fuel Economy by Car Model")

# Horizontal boxplot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Modern alternative: swap aes() directly (ggplot2 ≥ 3.3)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(y = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar()

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_polar() — pie / radar charts
coord_polar() maps one of the axes to the angle and the other to the radius.
library(ggplot2)

# Pie chart (theta = "y" maps y to angle)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(1), fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill = "Cylinders",
       title = "Cylinder distribution in mtcars")

# Coxcomb / Rose chart (theta = "x")
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(width = 1, colour = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "x") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Coxcomb chart by cylinder count")

# Radar / spider chart (with line geom)
# For proper radar charts use the fmsb or ggradar packages
# Quick approximation:
ggplot(mtcars[1, ], aes(x = "mpg", y = mpg)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.8) +
  coord_polar() +
  theme_minimal()

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_trans() — transform coordinates
Transforms the visual coordinate space (unlike scale_*_log10() which transforms the data before plotting).
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()

# Log10 Y axis
p + coord_trans(y = "log10")

# Square root on both axes
p + coord_trans(x = "sqrt", y = "sqrt")

# Log on X, reverse Y
p + coord_trans(x = "log10") + scale_y_reverse()

# Compare: scale_y_log10 (transforms data) vs coord_trans (transforms display)
p + scale_y_log10()                    # stat layers use log-transformed data
p + coord_trans(y = "log10")          # stat layers use original data

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_fixed() — fixed aspect ratio
Forces a fixed ratio between x and y units. Default ratio = 1 means one unit on x equals one unit on y.
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = qsec)) + geom_point()

# Default (free aspect ratio)
p

# 1:1 aspect ratio — one unit on y = one unit on x
p + coord_fixed()

# 2:1 — one unit on y = 2 units on x
p + coord_fixed(ratio = 2)

# Great for correlation matrices, maps, raster images
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  coord_fixed()

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
coord_equal() — equal units
Similar to coord_fixed(ratio = 1). Useful for geographic data and correlation plots.
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = mpg + rnorm(32))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "tomato") +
  coord_equal()

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
Reversing axes
library(ggplot2)

# Reverse the Y axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_reverse()

# Reverse the X axis
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_reverse()

# Both — with coord_cartesian zoom
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(35, 10))

title: Coordinate Systems
text:
Date / time coordinates
library(ggplot2)

# Zoom into a date range
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = as.Date(c("2000-01-01", "2015-01-01")))

# Custom date axis breaks and labels
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks  = "5 years",
    date_labels  = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed (thousands)",
       title = "US Unemployment 1967–2015")

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
ggplot2 is a powerful, open-source data visualization library for R developed by Hadley Wickham. It is based on the Grammar of Graphics — a systematic framework for describing any statistical graphic as a combination of layers.
One of ggplot2’s defining strengths is layered plot construction: start with data, map aesthetics, add geometric objects, then refine with scales, facets, and themes — each + call adds a new layer.
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)

The 7 Layers of Grammar of Graphics








Layer

Example

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
Aesthetics (aes)
The aes() function maps data variables to visual properties. There are two kinds:

Mapped (inside aes()) — value varies by data
Fixed (outside aes()) — constant for all data points

# MAPPED — colour changes per group
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# FIXED — all points are steelblue, size 3
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3, alpha = 0.7)

# BOTH — shape mapped to data, colour fixed
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(colour = "tomato", size = 3)

Aesthetic reference



Aesthetic
Maps to
Example




x
Horizontal axis position
aes(x = weight)


y
Vertical axis position
aes(y = height)


colour
Outline / point colour
aes(colour = species)


fill
Fill colour (bars, areas)
aes(fill = group)


size
Point size / line width
aes(size = population)


shape
Point shape (0–24)
aes(shape = type)


alpha
Transparency (0–1)
aes(alpha = confidence)


linetype
Solid / dashed / dotted
aes(linetype = group)


label
Text labels
aes(label = name)


group
Grouping without visual encoding
aes(group = id)

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
section: Building a Plot Step by Step
text:
Building a Plot Step by Step
library(ggplot2)

# Step 1: data + aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

# Step 2: add geometry
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Step 3: map colour to a third variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3)

# Step 4: add a smooth trend line
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

# Step 5: labels
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Weight vs MPG", colour = "Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)", y = "Miles per Gallon")

# Step 6: theme
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Weight vs MPG", colour = "Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)", y = "Miles per Gallon") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
Scales
Scales control how data values map to visual properties.
# Axis limits
scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 50), breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10))
scale_y_log10()
scale_x_date(date_labels = "%Y-%m")
scale_x_reverse()

# Colour & fill — continuous
scale_colour_gradient(low = "white", high = "darkred")
scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", midpoint = 0)

# Colour & fill — discrete
scale_colour_manual(values = c("#e84855", "#2d6be4", "#12a36a"))
scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")
scale_colour_viridis_d()          # colorblind-friendly

# Axis labels
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format())
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)
scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar)

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
Faceting
Faceting splits data into multiple sub-panels.
library(ggplot2)

# facet_wrap — one variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ gear)

# Custom rows / columns
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl, nrow = 1)

# Free scales per panel
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl, scales = "free")

# facet_grid — two variables
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(am ~ cyl)            # rows ~ columns

# Only column facets
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ cyl)

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
Key ggplot2 Functions
# Labels
labs(title = , subtitle = , caption = , x = , y = , colour = , fill = , tag = )
ggtitle("Title", subtitle = "Subtitle")
xlab("X axis")  ;  ylab("Y axis")

# Coordinates
coord_flip()                    # swap x and y
coord_polar(theta = "y")        # pie / radar charts
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,5))  # zoom without dropping data
coord_fixed()                   # equal unit lengths on both axes

# Annotations
annotate("text",  x = 2, y = 3, label = "Note")
annotate("rect",  xmin = 1, xmax = 2, ymin = 0, ymax = 5, alpha = 0.1)
annotate("segment", x = 1, y = 1, xend = 3, yend = 3, arrow = arrow())

# Theme shortcuts
theme_grey()       # default
theme_bw()         # black & white
theme_minimal()    # no background
theme_classic()    # axes only, no grid
theme_dark()       # dark panel
theme_void()       # blank canvas

# Set global theme
old <- theme_set(theme_minimal())
theme_set(old)     # restore

# Save
ggsave("plot.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)

title: ggplot2 — Introduction & Grammar of Graphics
text:
The theme() Function
The theme() function overrides any non-data visual element:
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(
    # Text elements
    plot.title        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle     = element_text(size = 12, colour = "grey50"),
    plot.caption      = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 1),
    axis.title        = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text         = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x       = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),

    # Panel
    panel.background  = element_rect(fill = "#f0f4f8"),
    panel.grid.major  = element_line(colour = "#dce3ec", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor  = element_blank(),
    panel.border      = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = NA),

    # Legend
    legend.position   = "top",
    legend.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),

    # Margins
    plot.margin       = margin(t = 20, r = 20, b = 20, l = 20)
  )

theme() element functions







Function
Used for




element_text(face, size, colour, hjust, vjust, angle)
Text elements


element_line(colour, linewidth, linetype)
Lines & grid


element_rect(fill, colour, linewidth)
Backgrounds & borders


element_blank()
Remove an element










TipTip — save & store your theme



Create a custom theme object once and reuse it across all your plots:
my_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )

# Apply to any plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  my_theme

Default position is "right". Use theme(legend.position = ...) to change it.
# Top

  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Set legend.position to a vector c(x, y) where both values are between 0 and 1 (fraction of the plot area).

  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme(

text:
Sample plots
Create four plots to combine throughout this page:
library(ggplot2)

mtcars -> df

# p1: Box plot
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = "", y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "p1 — Boxplot")

# p2: Normal density curve
p2 <- ggplot() +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, geom = "density",
                xlim = c(-3, 3), fill = "#f87060", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "p2 — Normal density")

# p3: Line chart
p3 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = mpg, y = disp)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "p3 — Line chart")

# p4: Scatter plot
p4 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = hp, y = wt)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "p4 — Scatter")

p1; p2; p3; p4

title: Combining Plots
text:
patchwork
install.packages("patchwork")
library(patchwork)

Basic operators
# + (or |) — side by side
p1 + p2
p1 | p2

# / — stacked (vertical)
p1 / p2

# 4 plots in auto-layout
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4

# Complex nesting
(p1 | p2) / p3           # two on top, one wide at bottom
p1 | (p2 / p3)            # one at left, two stacked at right
p1 + ((p2 | p3) / p4)     # nested 3-panel right side


plot_layout() — control layout
# Set number of columns
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)

# Relative widths and heights
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1), heights = c(1, 2))

# Custom design string
# 1,2,3,4 = plot numbers; # = empty space
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_layout(design = "
    111
    2#3
    443
  ")


wrap_plots() — for lists of plots
# When you don't know the number of plots at coding time
wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3, p4,
           ncol    = 2,
           nrow    = 2,
           widths  = c(1, 0.5),
           heights = c(0.5, 1))

# From a list (e.g. from lapply)
plot_list <- list(p1, p2, p3, p4)
wrap_plots(plot_list, ncol = 2)


plot_spacer() — add empty gaps
p1 + plot_spacer() + p3         # p1 | gap | p3

# Multi-row with spacers
(p1 + plot_spacer() + p2) /
(p3 + p4 + plot_spacer())


plot_annotation() — overall title & panel labels
# Overall title, subtitle, caption
p1 + ((p2 | p3) / p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Combined plot title",
    subtitle = "A subtitle for the whole figure",
    caption  = "Source: mtcars dataset"
  )

# Automatic panel labels
p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")    # A, B, C…

p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "1")    # 1, 2, 3, 4

# Labels with prefix
p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A",
                  tag_prefix = "Fig. ")   # Fig. A, Fig. B

# Roman numerals
p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "i")    # i, ii, iii…


& operator — apply to all panels
# Set same theme for all plots at once
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 & theme_minimal()

# Combined with annotation
(p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 & theme_minimal()) +
  plot_annotation(title = "All with theme_minimal")


Add new layers to a patchwork
# Adds to the LAST plot in the patchwork
p2 + p1 + geom_jitter(colour = "tomato")

# Access specific plot by index
patch <- p2 + p1
patch[[1]] <- patch[[1]] + theme_bw()
patch


Mix ggplot2 with base R plots
old_par <- par()
par(mar = c(0, 2, 0, 0), bg = NA)
p1 + wrap_elements(panel = ~ plot(1:10))
par(old_par)


Add a table (with gridExtra)
library(gridExtra)

tab <- t(round(quantile(mtcars$mpg), 2))
p1 / tableGrob(tab)


Add text annotations
library(grid)

p1 + textGrob("Text at the right")
wrap_elements(textGrob("Text at the left")) + p1

text:
Example 2 — ggplot2 basic bar chart
library(ggplot2)

Vertical (default)
# stat = "identity" — use y values as-is
ggplot(df1, aes(x = group, y = values)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

# geom_col() is shorthand for geom_bar(stat = "identity")
ggplot(df1, aes(x = group, y = values)) +
  geom_col()


Horizontal with coord_flip()
ggplot(df1, aes(x = group, y = values)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  coord_flip()


Sorted horizontal bars
ggplot(df1, aes(x = values, y = reorder(group, values))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Values", y = "Group")


With colours and legend
ggplot(df1, aes(x = group, y = values, fill = group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#e84855","#2d6be4","#12a36a","#d4a017")) +
  theme_minimal()


With value labels
ggplot(df1, aes(x = group, y = values, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = values), vjust = -0.4, fontface = "bold") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


stat = “count” (count rows, no y mapping needed)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Number of Cylinders") +
  labs(y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

text:
Example 3 — Stacked bar chart
Stacked bars show how subgroups contribute to a total. Map fill to the subgroup variable.
ggplot(df2, aes(x = maingroup, y = values, fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

Styled stacked chart
ggplot(df2, aes(x = maingroup, y = values, fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("a" = "#2d6be4", "b" = "#e84855")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = values),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Stacked Bar Chart",
       x = "Group", y = "Values", fill = "Subgroup") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Bar Charts (5 Examples)
text:
Example 4 — 100% stacked (proportional)
Scale all bars to the same height to compare proportions across groups.

Scaled to 1.0
ggplot(df2, aes(x = maingroup, y = values, fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill")
# Y axis shows 0.00 – 1.00


Scaled to 100%
library(scales)

ggplot(df2, aes(x = maingroup, y = values, fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(y = "Percentage") +
  theme_minimal()


With percentage labels inside bars
library(dplyr)
library(scales)

df2_pct <- df2 |>
  group_by(maingroup) |>
  mutate(pct = values / sum(values))

ggplot(df2_pct, aes(x = maingroup, y = values, fill = subgroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("a" = "#2d6be4", "b" = "#e84855")) +
  labs(title = "100% Stacked Bar Chart", y = "Proportion") +
  theme_minimal()

Grouped bars place subgroups side by side. Use position = "dodge".

Fine-tune gap between bars

  geom_bar(stat = "identity",

           width    = 0.7) +

            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
            vjust    = -0.4,

text:
Setting a global theme
Use theme_set() to apply a theme to all subsequent plots in your session:
library(ggplot2)

# Save current theme and set a new one
old <- theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

# Now ALL plots use theme_minimal
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Width)) + geom_histogram()

# Restore the previous theme
theme_set(old)

title: Themes & Styling
text:
Custom theme with theme()
Build your own reusable theme:
library(ggplot2)

my_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Titles
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                                   colour = "#0e0f14", margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(colour = "#6b6760", size = 12,
                                   margin = margin(b = 12)),
    plot.caption    = element_text(colour = "#aaaaaa", size = 9, hjust = 1),

    # Axes
    axis.title      = element_text(size = 11, colour = "#3d3e47"),
    axis.text       = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#6b6760"),
    axis.line       = element_line(colour = "#d8d2c8"),

    # Grid
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#ede8df", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#faf8f4", colour = NA),
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", colour = NA),

    # Legend
    legend.position  = "top",
    legend.title     = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text      = element_text(size = 10),

    # Facet strips
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),

    # Margins
    plot.margin      = margin(16, 16, 16, 16)
  )

# Apply to any plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#e84855","#2d6be4","#12a36a")) +
  labs(title = "Custom Theme", colour = "Cylinders") +
  my_theme
